There's no equivalent in PyTorch to the Keras' Input. All you have to do is pass on the inputs as a tensor to the PyTorch model.

For eg: If you're working with a Conv net:

input_tensor = torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32) # An input tensor of shape BatchSizexChannelsxHeightxWidth

The `tf.keras.Input` function is used to create an input layer for a model.
It can be used as follows:

```
input_layer = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,))
x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu')(input_layer)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=input_layer, outputs=x)
```

In this example, `input_layer` is the input layer and `x` is the output layer.

No gradients are propagated to the generator, as no calculation was performed with any of the generator's parameters. The discriminator being in eval mode would not prevent the gradients from propagating to the generator, albeit they would be slightly different if you are using layers that behave differently in eval mode compared to train mode, such as dropout.

The misclassification of real images is not part of training the generator, because it doesn't gain anything from this information. Conceptually, what should the generator learn from the fact that the discriminator failed to correctly classify a real image? The sole task of the generator is to create a fake image such that the discriminator thinks it's real, therefore the only relevant information for the generator is whether the discriminator was able to identify the fake image. If the discriminator was indeed able to identify the fake image, the generator needs to adjust itself to create a more convincing fake.

Of course it's not a binary case, but the generator always tries to improve the fake image such that the discriminator is even more convinced that it was a real image. The generator's goal is not to make the discriminator be doubtful (probability of 0.5 that it's real or fake), but that the discriminator is fully convinced that it's real, even though it's fake. That's why they are adversarial, not cooperative.

The discriminator is not used to train the generator, so you don't need to set it to `eval()` mode.

In order to update the generator, you should:

- Set the discriminator to `eval()` mode.
- Set the generator to `train()` mode.
- Compute the loss using the real samples.

- Call `optimizer_generator.step()`.

### Fake Implementations of PyTorch Operators 

Recall that during tracing, we are executing the program with [fake Tensors](https://localhost:8000/docs/main/torch.compiler_fake_tensor.html)  ,
which have no data. In general we cannot call the actual implementations of
PyTorch operators with fake Tensors. Thus each operator needs to have an
additional fake (a.k.a. “meta”) implementation, which inputs and outputs fake
Tensors, that matches the behavior of the actual implementation in terms of
shapes and other forms of metadata carried by fake Tensors. 

For example, note how the fake implementation of [`torch.index_select()`](generated/torch.index_select.html#torch.index_select "torch.index_select")  computes the shape of the output using the shape of the input (while ignoring
input data and returning empty output data). 

```
def meta_index_select(self, dim, index):
    result_size = list(self.size())
    if self.dim() > 0:
        result_size[dim] = index.numel()
    return self.new_empty(result_size)

```

#### Shape Propagation: Backed vs. Unbacked Dynamic Shapes 

Shapes are propagated using fake implementations of PyTorch operators. 

A key concept to understand the propagation of dynamic shapes in particular
is the difference between *backed*  and *unbacked*  dynamic shapes: we know the
concrete values of the former but not the latter. 

Propagation of shapes, including tracking backed and unbacked dynamic shapes,

If your network has multiple losses, you must call `scaler.scale`  on each of them individually.
If your network has multiple optimizers, you may call `scaler.unscale_`  on any of them individually,
and you must call `scaler.step`  on each of them individually. 

However, `scaler.update`  should only be called once,
after all optimizers used this iteration have been stepped:

scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler()

for epoch in epochs:
    for input, target in data:
        optimizer0.zero_grad()
        optimizer1.zero_grad()
        with autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.float16):
            output0 = model0(input)
            output1 = model1(input)
            loss0 = loss_fn(2 * output0 + 3 * output1, target)
            loss1 = loss_fn(3 * output0 - 5 * output1, target)

        # (retain_graph here is unrelated to amp, it's present because in this
        # example, both backward() calls share some sections of graph.)
        scaler.scale(loss0).backward(retain_graph=True)
        scaler.scale(loss1).backward()

        # You can choose which optimizers receive explicit unscaling, if you
        # want to inspect or modify the gradients of the params they own.

In this context, this means that the (implicitly declared) computation graphs will be kept alive as long as there are references to the objects holding them in the current scope!

This means that if you e.g. do some kind of batching on samples s_1 ... s_k, compute the loss for each and add the loss at the end, that cumulative loss will hold references to each individual loss, which in turn holds references to each of the computation nodes that computed it.

I think you're misunderstanding what Seq2Seq is about. It's not about applying a model on a sequence of length N, but rather training a model that takes as input a sequence of length N and produces another sequence of length M.

In your case, you have two sequences: one for the source text (the long one) and one for the summary (the short one). You can train a Seq2Seq model with these two sequences. The encoder will take the source text and produce a fixed-length vector (or a sequence of vectors if you use LSTM), which will then be used by the decoder to generate the summary.

The attention mechanism is just a way to make the decoder more efficient when generating the summary. Instead of using only the last hidden state from the encoder, the decoder uses all the hidden states produced by the encoder, giving higher weights to the most relevant ones. This allows the decoder to focus on different parts of the source text while generating each word of the summary.

`zero_grad()` clears out the gradients computed from the last step. If you don't do this, the gradient would be accumulated to existing gradients.

The problem here is that you're using `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` incorrectly.

Firstly, `CrossEntropyLoss` expects the input to be unnormalized scores (often referred to as logits) for each class. It then computes and normalizes these into probabilities via softmax before computing the negative log likelihood loss. This means that you don't need to manually apply softmax to your predictions.

Secondly, `CrossEntropyLoss` expects the target to be a tensor of class indices, not one-hot encoded vectors. You can use [`torch.argmax`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#torch.argmax) on your one-hot encoded targets to convert them to class indices.

So, assuming that `y_pred` contains unnormalized scores for each class, you should do:

loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

Explanation:

`torch.log()` computes the natural logarithm of `output`. Since `output` is a probability distribution, it's values are between 0 and 1. Therefore, their logaritms are negative. This means that the closer the predicted probability is to zero, the higher the loss will be. For example, if the model predicts a 10% chance of rain, but the actual result was sunny, the loss would be `-ln(0.1)` ≈ 2.3. On the other hand, if the model predicts a 90% chance of rain, but the actual result was sunny, the loss would be `-ln(0.9)` ≈ 0.1. So, the lower the predicted probability, the higher the loss.

In addition, the loss is normalized by dividing it by the number of elements in `target`, i.e., the number of correct predictions. This ensures that the loss remains constant regardless of the number of correct predictions.

The `reduction` argument of [`F.cross_entropy`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy.html#torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy) is used to specify what should be done with the losses computed for each element of the batch.

- `'none'`: no reduction will be applied, i.e., the output is simply the loss per sample.
- `'mean'`: the mean of the individual losses is taken.
- `'sum'`: the output will be summed.

I think you have misunderstood what `DataParallel` does.

When you wrap your model with `DataParallel`, it will copy the model to all the GPUs that you specified (in this case, just one), and then it will do the forward pass in parallel across all of them. The backward pass will be done sequentially, though, because gradients can only be computed on the CPU.

So, if you want to train on multiple GPUs, you should use `DataParallel`. If you want to test on a single GPU, you don't need to use `DataParallel`.

If you want to save memory during inference, you could try using [`torch.no_grad()`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/autograd.html#torch.no_grad) instead of wrapping your model with `DataParallel`. This will prevent the creation of intermediate variables during the forward pass, which might help reduce peak memory usage. However, you won't be able to compute gradients while doing inference this way.

You can use any Python object as a parameter, so long as it supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and indexing.
